fieldMarks: Washington's largest woodland salamander: about 2.5-3 inches snout-vent, 5.5-6 inches total.
Tan, yellow or green dorsal stripe over a dark black or brown body; juveniles have a brighter stripe.
Stripe does not reach the tail tip and has an uneven 'eroding' edge invaded by blotches of the side colour.
Sides have patchy blotches and flecks the colour of the stripe; usually 15 costal grooves.
Nasolabial grooves separate it from non-plethodontid salamanders such as the long-toed salamander.
behavior: Active above ground mostly at night during or after rain, mainly spring and fall in Washington; hard to find in the dry summer.
Eats small invertebrates including mites, springtails, snails and flies.
Eggs are laid on land in clusters of roughly 4-18 in moist crevices, rotted logs or cavities; no free-living larval stage.
Hides under rocks, logs, moss and leaf litter; may enter water to escape predators.
habitat: Shaded, rocky edges of humid forested streams, stream seepages and moist talus slopes; moss-covered outcrops.
Needs cool, permanently moist conditions but not flowing water.
range: Southwestern Washington (Willapa Hills) south through western Oregon to extreme northwestern California (Smith River watershed), from sea level to about 1,000 m.

lookalikes.name: Western red-backed salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: Lacks blotches and flecks of the stripe colour on the sides of the body.

lookalikes.name: Long-toed salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: No nasolabial grooves, rounded snout, noticeably longer fourth hind toe.
